name: Olympian religion in Homer
plain_explanation: The gods of Homer's epics are essentially glorified human conquerors: not moral models, immortal and powerful but otherwise all-too-human, quarrelsome, and capable of favoritism and deceit.
precise_definition: The polytheistic religion depicted in Homer, in which the Olympian gods are anthropomorphic conquerors of the world rather than its creators, morally unedifying, and less religiously serious (in Russell's view) than the darker, more primitive cults that persisted alongside them.
why_it_mattered: Russell treats Homer as an 'expurgator' who suppressed cruder popular superstitions in favor of an upper-class ideal of urbane enlightenment, which explains why later, more primitive beliefs kept resurfacing throughout classical Greek history.
historical_origin: Crystallized in the Homeric poems, composed and edited over roughly two centuries, reaching their fixed form by the sixth century B.C.
examples: Gilbert Murray's description of the Olympians as 'conquering chieftains, royal buccaneers' who do no useful work
The immoral, feuding House of Pelops (Tantalos, Pelops, Atreus, Thyestes, Agamemnon, Orestes)
competing_positions: The darker, tribal fertility religions (e.g. the cult of Pan in Arcadia) that persisted beneath the Homeric surface
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The Homeric gods reflect the outlook of a conquering aristocracy rather than of the agricultural population, and Homer's poems became the core of Athenian education from the time of Peisistratus onward.
